cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Fair Exchange
cards.instruction: Price every favor in time, effort, inconvenience, or future obligation.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. Half an hour helping you move buys two hours painting my shed on Saturday.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Saturday's my only lie-in. Can I come after lunch?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Afternoon painting costs me cricket. Three hours, then.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I'll hire a painter. But I need the sofa carried up three flights.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Then two painter-hours covers loading; the stairs cost a third. Cricket's free again.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 sets labor equivalence, A3 delays B timing challenge and raises the rate for lost cricket, and A5 reprices purchased labor after B adds stairs.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 afternoon request costs A cricket in A3; B4 hired painter restores that time but adds lifting effort, causing A5 two hours plus one.

relationship.evidence: B2 protects a lie-in and B4 offers outsourced repayment while clarifying the move, plausibly negotiating a practical exchange.

heightening.evidence: B4 changes both repayment form and task scope, so A5 separates loading from stair effort while reclaiming leisure.

specificity.evidence: A1 half-hour move and shed painting, B2 Saturday rest and B4 three flights establish concrete traded burdens.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 cricket-free-again follows the hired painter solution rather than an unrelated reward.
